options: A data modeling technique for structuring data as fact and dimension tables for fast, intuitive analytical queries
A specific diagram shape that all warehouses must use
A synonym for normalization
A Power BI-only feature with no application in a data warehouse
questions.explain: Dimensional modeling is the underlying technique — classifying every table as a fact or a dimension and designing each accordingly. Star and snowflake are shapes it can produce, not the definition itself.

questions.q: What are the only two table types a dimensional model ever produces?
options: Fact tables and dimension tables
Staging tables and archive tables
Primary tables and secondary tables
Cube tables and report tables
questions.explain: Every table in a dimensional model is classified as either a fact table (measurements/events) or a dimension table (descriptive business entities) — never a mix of both.

questions.q: Which columns belong in a dimension table?
options: A key column plus descriptive attribute columns used for filtering and grouping
Only numeric measures meant to be summed
Only foreign keys, with no attributes at all
Raw transaction logs from the OLTP source
questions.explain: Dimension tables describe business entities (products, customers, dates) with a unique key plus descriptive attributes analysts filter and group by.

questions.q: What does dimensional modeling deliberately trade away, and for what?
options: Storage space and write-time simplicity, in exchange for read-time query performance and simplicity
Data accuracy, in exchange for faster development
Security, in exchange for easier reporting
Nothing — dimensional models have no tradeoffs compared to normalized schemas
questions.explain: Dimensional models are deliberately denormalized: the same descriptive values are repeated across rows, trading storage and write-time complexity for dramatically simpler, faster analytical reads.

questions.q: According to Microsoft's own guidance, why does this course build the dimensional model as real ETL-loaded warehouse tables rather than a Power Query-only semantic model?
options: Only a warehouse loaded by ETL can properly track historical change (Slowly Changing Dimensions), which a Power Query-only model can't do
Power BI cannot connect to warehouse tables at all
ETL-loaded tables are always smaller than Power Query tables
There is no difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: A Power Query-defined semantic model can mimic dimensional structure, but it can't manage historical change the way a periodically-loaded warehouse dimension table can — exactly the SCD problem Chapters 3-4 cover.
